title: Šuppiluliuma I
wiki_lead:
Šuppiluliuma I (died c. 1322 BC), also Suppiluliuma () or Suppiluliumas (), was an ancient Hittite king (r. c. 1350–1322 BC).
Even before assuming the throne, Šuppiluliuma distinguished himself as a military commander by protecting and reclaiming Hittite territories after a period of foreign attacks. Once becoming king he continued his program of consolidation and expansion, both in Anatolia and Syria, with a great deal of success. Victories over a major rival, the Upper-Mesopotamian kingdom of Mittani, led to the extension of Hittite authority over a bevy of petty kingdoms in northern Syria, the installation of the Hittite king's younger sons as local viceroys at Aleppo and Carchemish, and the rump of the Mittanian state becoming, effectively, a dependency of the Hittite Kingdom.
Relations with Egypt vacillated between friendship and hostility, eventually culminating in the Zannanza Affair in which Šuppiluliuma was persuaded to send one of his sons to marry the widowed queen of Egypt and assume its throne. However, the murder of this Hittite prince resulted in a long period of Hittite-Egyptian hostility, and captives that Šuppiluliuma had taken caused an outbreak of plague which ravaged Hittite society for at least two decades. Despite all his successes, Šuppiluliuma's son, Muršili II, blamed the Hittite's misfortune as being the result of his father's cruelty.

Origins
Šuppiluliuma's origins are unclear. A statement in the genealogy of his grandson Ḫattušili III was long taken to indicate that Šuppiluliuma’s father, and Ḫattušili III's great-grandfather, was Ḫattušili II. However, the terminology involved (which when taken literally would indicate that Ḫattušili III was the great-grandson of Ḫattušili II) might have indicated more distant descent, and the Ḫattušili in question might have been the famous Ḫattušili I at the dawn of Hittite power in the late 17th century BC. The discovery of seal impressions naming Šuppiluliuma as the son of Tudḫaliya III (sometimes called II) led to the discarding of the previous hypothesis by most scholars. Most scholars now concluded that Šuppiluliuma was the son of his predecessor, Tudḫaliya III, whom he had long served as a military commander. However, the description of Šuppiluliuma's first wife Ḫenti as the "great queen, daughter of the great king, the hero," has resulted in her identification as the daughter of Tudḫaliya III, making Šuppiluliuma the son-in-law and possibly adopted son of that king.


Generalship

According to the Deeds of Šuppiluliuma composed by his son and second successor Muršili II, Šuppiluliuma served as the adviser and chief military commander to his predecessor Tudḫaliya III, helping effect the king's recovery of his lands from Šamuḫa, where the court had established itself for greater security from enemy attack.
Tudḫaliya and Šuppiluliuma waged a successful campaign against the Kaška in the north, then intervened to recover control over and protect the regions of Kaššiya and the Ḫulana River Land to the west and southwest, striking back at their invaders. After dealing with a new threat from the Kaška under Piyapili, Tudḫaliya and Šuppiluliuma, had to fight King Karanni (or Lanni) of Azzi-Ḫayaša in the northeast. Karanni had invaded Hittite territory and even threatened Šamuḫa, but was defeated, Tudḫaliya and Šuppiluliuma invading Azzi-Ḫayaša in turn. A battle at Kummaḫa (probably Kemah) seems to have resulted in a Hittite victory, as Azzi-Ḫayaša is later found as a Hittite vassal.
After these successes in the north, Tudḫaliya seems to have been able to return to the Hittite capital, Ḫattuša. He sent Šuppiluliuma southwest against the Arzawa confederacy, and Šuppiluliuma was victorious in several battles, recovering the city of Tuwanuwa (probably Tyana), which had been occupied by the enemy.

grok_lead: Å uppiluliuma I (c. 1350â1322 BC) was a Hittite king who ruled the kingdom of Hatti during the height of its imperial phase in the Late Bronze Age, transforming it into a dominant power in Anatolia and the Near East through relentless military expansion and strategic vassalage. As the son of Tudhaliya II, he ascended the throne after a period of internal strife, defeating the faction led by his rival relative Tudhaliya the Younger (later designated Tudhaliya III) in a coup supported by the military, thereby consolidating royal authority amid threats from neighboring powers. His reign is marked by a series of calculated campaigns that first secured Hittite control over western and northern Anatolian rivals, including the subjugation of Arzawa and Hayasa-Azzi, before pivoting to devastating incursions into northern Syria and the Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni, capturing key cities like Aleppo and Kadesh and installing his son Piyassili as viceroy in Carchemish to administer the new territories. These conquests not only reclaimed lost lands but extended Hittite influence toward Egypt, culminating in tentative diplomatic overtures, such as the proposed marriage alliance with the widow of Tutankhamun, which tragically introduced a plague that decimated the royal family, including several of his sons. Å uppiluliuma's legacy as an empire-builder endures, with his policies laying the foundation for the subsequent reigns of his successors, though reliant on fragile alliances and constant vigilance against rebellion. The principal historical record of his accomplishments derives from the Deeds of Å uppiluliuma, a detailed annalistic account composed by his son and successor Mursili II, which, despite its propagandistic tone inherent to royal inscriptions, provides indispensable empirical detail on campaigns, treaties, and administrative innovations drawn from cuneiform archives at Hattusa. This text, supplemented by diplomatic correspondence and seals, underscores Å uppiluliuma's role in pioneering Hittite imperial diplomacy, including vassal treaties that enforced loyalty through oaths and mutual obligations, reflecting a pragmatic realism in balancing conquest with governance.
